title: RP1: An Open Source Full-Stack Platform for Agentic Humanoids
content:
English / 简体中文
  From mechanical design and electronics to firmware, control and learning.
Built to be understood. Open to be built upon.
RP1 is RoboParty's fully open-source humanoid platform: a shared foundation for building, understanding and extending a real robot.
The platform brings mechanical and electrical design, joint modules, firmware, robot models, deployment and learning into one connected development stack. Explore a single subsystem, reproduce a build, or develop your own control and learning workflows.
RP1, photographed in the real world.
No black boxes, nothing withheld — full control handed back to the developer
Release contents, supported configurations and setup instructions are maintained in each repository.
Contributions belong in the relevant sub-repository. This overview repository does not accept pull requests; please open issues and pull requests in the project you are working on.
Robot configurations
See the description repository's current release for supported robot configurations.
Supported configurations include 24, 28, 30 and 42 DoF variants.
Coming soon.

report.summary: RoboParty's RP1 is a fully open-source full-stack humanoid platform spanning mechanical design, electronics, firmware, control and learning, offered in 24 to 42 DoF configurations.
report.background: Humanoid robotics has shifted from lab spectacle to a genuine engineering race, but the most capable systems remain closed: Boston Dynamics, Figure, Tesla Optimus and most Chinese vendors publish demos while withholding CAD, firmware and control stacks. That secrecy makes reproducibility nearly impossible for outside researchers, who must reverse-engineer torque limits, joint dynamics and communication buses before writing a single line of control code. In parallel, the open-source ecosystem has matured — MuJoCo and Isaac Lab for simulation, LeRobot for learning pipelines, ROS 2 for middleware — yet a complete, honest hardware reference has been missing. RP1 emerges from RoboParty with GPL-3.0 licensing, modular sub-repositories, and a research pipeline (P-BFM, I-BFM, PredActor, INTACT, VIStream) targeting ICLR and ICRA, positioning it as both a buildable robot and a reproducible research baseline for unsupervised reinforcement learning on humanoids.
key_points: RP1 is not a single product but a connected development stack: mechanical and electrical design, joint modules, firmware, robot models, deployment tooling and learning workflows each live in their own repository, so developers can study one subsystem or reproduce the entire machine.

RoboParty explicitly markets the platform as having 'no black boxes, nothing withheld,' pitching it against the proprietary humanoid stacks that dominate the current commercial landscape and handing full control back to the developer.

Supported configurations span 24, 28, 30 and 42 degrees of freedom, letting teams choose between a simpler, cheaper research biped and a full upper-body-plus-hands platform, with additional configurations promised as 'coming soon.'

The release is backed by an unusually deep academic pipeline: P-BFM and I-BFM push unsupervised reinforcement learning for perceptive humanoid control and interaction, while PredActor, INTACT and VIStream tackle onboard diffusion control, world models and inertial sensing in streaming geometric foundation models.

Governance is deliberately modular: issues and pull requests belong in the relevant sub-repository, the overview repo accepts none, and licensing is per-repository under a GPL-3.0 umbrella — a structure that keeps contributions traceable but asks contributors to learn the project's hierarchy.
report.impact: For the AI industry, RP1 threatens the assumption that humanoid competence requires proprietary hardware stacks; if the platform is genuinely reproducible, it becomes a shared benchmark where control and learning results can be compared across labs rather than across marketing videos. For developers, it lowers the entry barrier dramatically — hobbyists, university labs and startups can now fork mechanical designs, flash firmware and train policies on a machine whose dynamics are publicly documented, mirroring what LeRobot and Isaac Lab did for manipulation and simulation. For regular users, the near-term effect is indirect: cheaper, more diverse humanoid hardware entering warehouses, labs and eventually homes, plus a faster cadence of public demonstrations. The main risk is fragmentation, since open hardware projects historically struggle with documentation, supply chains and long-term maintenance.
report.tools: Follow RP1's sub-repositories directly on GitHub alongside Isaac Lab and MuJoCo for simulation, ROS 2 for middleware, and Hugging Face LeRobot for learning pipelines. The cited papers — P-BFM, I-BFM, PredActor, INTACT and VIStream — are worth reading for the underlying unsupervised RL and diffusion-control methods. Comparable open-hardware efforts to track include Unitree's SDK ecosystem and K-Scale Labs, which make useful reference points when evaluating RP1's documentation and buildability.
